meta.title: The central limit theorem in noise: why interference becomes Gaussian
meta.tools: Sums of N non-Gaussian interferers (uniform-phase sinusoids, impulsive Bernoulli–Gaussian, binary), excess kurtosis vs N, Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance and the Berry–Esseen rate
meta.summary: Add up N independent non-Gaussian interference sources and measure how quickly the sum becomes Gaussian — excess kurtosis falls as 1/N and the maximum CDF error as 1/√N — and show why impulsive noise converges much more slowly.
meta.problem: Receivers are designed for Gaussian noise even though no individual interferer is Gaussian. When is that justified?
meta.theory:
For i.i.d. terms with excess kurtosis κ, the normalised sum has excess kurtosis κ/N. Berry–Esseen: $\sup|F_N-Φ| \le C\frac{ρ}{σ^3\sqrt N}$ (C < 0.48, ρ = E|X|³). A random-phase sinusoid (arcsine law) has κ = −1.5;
impulsive noise (Gaussian present with probability 0.01, variance 100) has κ ≈ 3/0.01 − 3 ≈ 297, so it needs ~100× more terms to look Gaussian.
meta.method: N = 1…1000 terms, 200,000 samples per N. Excess kurtosis vs κ/N; KS distance to N(0,1) vs N; Berry–Esseen bound computed for each distribution.
